summary:
Cognate prediction and proto-form reconstruction are key tasks in computational historical linguistics that rely on the study of sound change regularity. Solving these tasks appears to be very similar to machine translation, though methods from that field have barely been applied to historical linguistics. Therefore, in this paper, we investigate the learnability of sound correspondences between a proto-language and daughter languages for two machine-translation-inspired models, one statistical, the other neural.
We first carry out our experiments on plausible artificial languages, without noise, in order to study the role of each parameter on the algorithms respective performance under almost perfect conditions. We then study real languages, namely Latin, Italian and Spanish, to see if those performances generalise well. We show that both model types manage to learn sound changes despite data scarcity, although the best performing model type depends on several parameters such as the size of the training data, the ambiguity, and the prediction direction.
title: Comparing Statistical and Neural Models for Learning Sound Correspondences

summary: Diachronic lexical information is not only important in the field of historical linguistics, but is also increasingly used in NLP, most recently for machine translation of low resource languages. Therefore, there is a need for fine-grained, large-coverage and accurate etymological lexical resources. In this paper, we propose a set of guidelines to generate such resources, for each step of the life-cycle of an etymological lexicon: creation, update, evaluation, dissemination, and exploitation. To illustrate the guidelines, we introduce EtymDB 2.0, an etymological database automatically generated from the Wiktionary, which contains 1.8 million lexemes, linked by more than 700,000 fine-grained etymological relations, across 2,536 living and dead languages. We also introduce use cases for which EtymDB 2.0 could represent a key resource, such as phylogenetic tree generation, low resource machine translation or medieval languages study.
title: Methodological Aspects of Developing and Managing an Etymological Lexical Resource: Introducing EtymDB 2.0

## For multilingual-translation architecture experiments
MEDeA (Multiway Encoder Decoder Architecture) is a fully parametrizable software for translation experiments on small datasets. Can also be used in historical linguistics for cognate prediction.

For a use case, see all my publications.
title: MEDeA

summary: Cognate and proto-form prediction are key tasks in computational historical linguistics, which rely heavily on sound correspondences identification, and could help low resource translation. In the last two decades, a combination of sequence alignement, statistical models and clustering methods have emerged to try and solve these. But where are the neural networks? In this talk, I will present my ongoing research in investigating the learnability of sound correspondences between a proto-language and daughter languages by neural models.  I will introduce: - MEDeA, a Multiway Encoder Decoder Architecture inspired by NMT, - EtymDB2.0, the etymological database that we updated to generate much needed data, - our experiments on plausible artificial languages as well as on real languages.
title: Learning Sound Correspondences: What about Neural Networks?

summary:
## Etymological database
This fine grained etymological database is extracted from a 2019 Wiktionary dump. It differentiates between inheritance, cognacy, borrowing, and different types of composition.

It is provided with several scripts for data analysis, including one to draw your own language trees from the word links.

_I contributed to the extraction of the 2019 dump, duplicate management in v2 of the base, and all the extraction scripts and notebooks present in the repo - the original Perl scripts were developed by [B. Sagot](http://alpage.inria.fr/~sagot/)_
title: EtymDB 2

summary:
## For neurodegenerative diseases prediction
LEASP (Learning Spatiotemporal Patterns) is a C++ tool to estimate the group average and individual spatio-temporal trajectories of patients with neurodegenerative diseases.

_Logic coded by [I. Koval](https://igorkoval.com/). I carried out the user interface, industrialisation (CI, coded the test suite), documentation, and dissemination (Docker packaging and work presentation to the Human Brain Project partners)._


LEASP has since then been ported to Python/Pytorch, go [check LEASPy out](https://gitlab.com/icm-institute/aramislab/leaspy), it's quite cool! [Introductory article by I. Koval on Medium](https://medium.com/@igoroa/analysis-of-longitudinal-data-made-easy-with-leaspy-f8d529fcb5f8)
title: LEASP

summary:
## For phonetic historical conlanging
If you want to try conlanging, you can with PLexGen, my phonetic lexicon generator and sound change applier! This little software is parametrizable, with json files to provide your language shape (phonetics and phonotactics) and text files to provide your sound changes.

It will then generate randomly a proto-language and its n daughter languages after your specifications.
title: PLexGen
